title: Wolves Are Back in Yellowstone — and They're a Big Deal!
summary:
Have you ever seen a wolf? They're amazing animals that live in family groups called packs. They work together to hunt big animals like elk. But did you know that wolves were once almost wiped out in the United States?

Long ago, wolves roamed all over North America. But when settlers came, they saw wolves as a threat. They trapped, shot, and poisoned them. By 1926, the last wolves in Yellowstone National Park were killed. The park even used poison called strychnine, which is really painful for animals.

For almost 70 years, there were no wolves in Yellowstone. But in 1995, scientists brought them back! They captured wolves from Canada and released them in the park. It was a big deal because wolves are top predators — they help keep the ecosystem balanced.

Without wolves, elk numbers grew too high, and they ate too many plants. With wolves back, the elk behave differently, and the whole park is healthier.

Now, Yellowstone is the best place in the country to see wild wolves. People go on tours for hours just to catch a glimpse of them. The park spans over 2.2 million acres across Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho.

Wolves are still a bit scary to some people, but they're also a cultural icon. One writer, Erica Berry, says that even a 'lone wolf' comes from a pack and is looking for another pack. So, wolves teach us about working together — pretty cool, right?
why_it_matters: Wolves show us that every animal has a job in nature, just like every kid plays a part in a team, and losing one species can change everything.

background_read: Yellowstone National Park (the world's first national park, famous for its geysers and wildlife) was home to hundreds of wolves before they were wiped out.
In the early 1900s, many wolves were killed across America because people feared they would attack livestock or people.
Bringing wolves back to Yellowstone in 1995 was a major conservation success story that helped restore the park's natural balance.
Article_Structure: WHO: Wolves (and the scientists who brought them back).
WHAT: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone after being missing for nearly 70 years.
WHERE: Yellowstone National Park, which spans 2.2 million acres across Wyoming, Montana, and Idaho.
WHY: To restore the ecosystem—without wolves, elk ate too many plants, and the whole park became unhealthy.

perspectives.description: They celebrate the wolves' return as a victory for protecting nature and bringing back a top predator that makes the park healthier.
Some farmers living near the park are concerned that wolves might attack their cattle or sheep.
They watch how the wolves change the park and use it as a real-world example of how predators keep ecosystems in check.
